articles.title: ’60 Minutes’ Kicks Off Much-Scrutinized 59th Season With Old Ticks, Tricks
articles.summary: CBS News says it needs to push “60 Minutes” into the future if the show is to survive, but the first telecast of the 59th season following a shocking overhaul of its on-air and behind-the-camera staff in May and June relied on many elements from the program’s past.
body: One of the stories even featured the old-time TV-news “hidden camera,” which many people thought went out of style after ABC News got sued in 1999 — and lost — for sending reporters to take footage at Food Lion supermarkets after lying on resumes and gaining access to tape unsanitary food practices. ABC News got tripped up on charges of trespassing and fraud, and hidden-camera reporting in the modern day is typically used mostly in public spaces or overseas, where U.S. laws don’t apply.

Will viewers miss Cecilia Vega, Sharyn Alfonsi, or Scott Pelley? The last of that trio, all pushed out of the show following the decision to oust top producers, was on nearly every week, often crashing a story tied to events that had taken place in the days leading up to broadcast.

Bari Weiss, the editor in chief of CBS News whose work at transforming the unit for modern audiences has stirred up a lot of controversy, wants “60 Minutes” to show up in more media venues and kick up livelier discussions. Other members of CBS News have felt this way as well, wondering if the program has gotten too soft or overly reliant on stories tied to the release of new books.

articles.title: Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation
articles.summary: Cynthia Erivo already earned two best actress Oscar nominations for portraying Harriet Tubman and the green-skinned Elphaba in “Wicked” — not to mention her Tony-winning work in “The Color Purple” — but her latest film, “Prima Facie,” might be her most challenging high-wire act yet.
body: White (“Bleak House,” “Jane Eyre,” “Woman Walks Ahead”) directed the adaptation by playwright Suzie Miller from her globally acclaimed one-woman show. The film is one of the hottest sales titles on the block at TIFF. Jodie Comer won the Tony and Olivier awards for the stage version, and Erivo proved equally captivating on the big screen — albeit under a the very racial and socioeconomic context. Erivo’s Tessa is a woman of color from a working class background, navigating a system bolstered by white men dating back to medieval times in the London court.

“We got the chance to meet a lot of Black women barristers. I understood that they sort of work in a different rhythm to everybody else, and the way they approach court is very much making it their own,” Erivo said at a Q&A following the premiere “I wanted that for Tessa, I wanted her to have this outside life that influenced the way she approached [her work].”

articles.title: Seth Green Says He Was Never Invited Back for the Canceled ‘Buffy the Vampire Slayer’ Reboot
articles.summary: Seth Green revealed in the Sept. 8 episode of “The McBride Rewind” podcast that he was not involved in any discussion of reprising his role as the werewolf guitarist Oz in Hulu’s canceled “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” reboot. “I was not part of those talks,” he said in the episode.
body: Reps for 20th Century and Hulu did not immediately respond to Variety ‘s request for comment.

The original seven-season series followed Sarah Michelle Gellar as Buffy Summers, a young woman who slays vampires, demons and other supernatural creatures with the help of her friends. Inspired by the film of the same title, “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” ran from 1997 to 2003. It was set to be rebooted by Hulu in March 2025 but was cancelled after the pilot.

The project, titled “Buffy the Vampire Slayer: New Sunnydale,” would have starred Ryan Kiera Armstrong as the new slayer, with original series star Gellar returning as Buffy. The pilot also starred Faly Rakotohavana as Hugo, Ava Jean as Larkin, Sarah Bock as Gracie, Daniel di Tomasso as Abe and Jack Cutmore-Scott as Mr. Burke.

articles.title: CBS Warns Humanity May Have a “Narrow Window” to Avoid AI Calamity, Right After ChatGPT Sponsors Its NFL Broadcast
articles.summary: ChatGPT was revealed as a surprise presenting sponsor of the 'NFL on CBS,' which was followed by '60 Minutes,' where one of its correspondents outlined a stark warning about the future if the technology remains unchecked.
body: CBS on Sunday night warned that the world may be sleepwalking toward a future where artificial intelligence runs amok, and perhaps destroys all of humanity.
For now, however, we will have to be content with the AI companies subsidizing our football broadcasts.
Videos online showed the broadcast booth during the New York Jets-Tennessee Titans game tossing to reporter Aditi Kinkhabwala, as the ChatGPT logo was displayed above the “Sideline Report” graphic.
The sponsorship underscores the lengths that big AI companies are going to secure power users, with OpenAI competitor Anthropic releasing memorable ads during this year’s Super Bowl as well.

articles.title: ‘Prima Facie’ Review: Cynthia Erivo Stars as a Lawyer Who Becomes a Rape Victim in This Misfire of an Adaptation
articles.summary: The Oscar nominee tackles the role originated by Jodie Comer on the West End and Broadway in Susanna White's film version of Suzie Miller's award-winning play.
body: Directed by Susanna White, whose smart works include the series Generation Kill and the thriller Our Kind of Traitor, the film opens with some of its heaviest-handed imagery. As Tessa bounces up the steps of the Old Bailey courthouse, already wearing her robe and white courtroom wig, the camera focuses on her out-of-place black-sequined sneakers. She steps into a room full of sleek, posh-looking women lawyers and in the first of her voiceovers, many taken directly from the play, says, “Thoroughbreds, that’s how I see them.” The film then cuts to images of — really, it’s this literal — horses.

Before long she has sex in the office with another rising-star lawyer, the privileged Julian. “I want this,” her unnecessary voiceover says. Julian is played with winning charm by Daniel Ings in a role that stretches him from his usual parts, like the buffoonish screw-up brother in the series The Gentlemen. Casting is not one of this film’s problems.
points: The Oscar nominee tackles the role originated by Jodie Comer on the West End and Broadway in Susanna White's film version of Suzie Miller's award-winning play.

articles.title: Israel’s Culture Minister Threatens to Revoke the Citizenship of ‘NAZA’ Filmmakers
articles.summary: Culture minister Miki Zohar said Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's documentary, which details the IDF's alleged systematic targeting and killing of civilians in Gaza, “constitutes treason.”
body: Israel ‘s Culture Minister has said he will work to revoke the citizenship of Oscar-winning filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor over their new documentary, NAZA.
Writing on X, Zohar described the film as “vile,” saying it “constitutes treason.”

“This is exactly the reason I led the important reform in cinema so that Israeli citizens will no longer have to pay out of their own pockets for the harm to IDF soldiers and the State of Israel,” Zohar wrote, referring to his recent reforms of government funding for the Israeli film industry.

NAZA, like the documentary No Other Land, directed by Zohar and Abraham together with Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, did not receive any Israeli public funding. NAZA was produced in part with support from British newspaper The Guardian.

articles.title: How Neil DeGrasse Tyson Really Feels About Project Hail Mary
articles.summary: Astrophysicist and frequent wet blanket Neil deGrasse Tyson often judges the accuracy of sci-fi movies. So what does he think about Project Hail Mary?
body: Is it any wonder that Neil deGrasse Tyson has found a kindred spirit in "Project Hail Mary" author Andy Weir? One is a professional stickler for scientific accuracy in works of fiction, and the other is the modern day savior of hard sci-fi. With that in mind, it should come as no surprise that Tyson has finally found a sci-fi movie with which he has little to no problem. Yep, "Project Hail Mary."

Bearing in mind this is the man who previously confronted Nobel prize-winning physicist Kip Thorne on his contribution to Christopher Nolan's "Interstellar," it's remarkable that what is essentially a live-action Pixar movie featuring a lovable pet rock sidekick has finally won him over. "Project Hail Mary" became a box office hit and easily one of the best sci-fi movies of 2026 without sacrificing hard science in favor of more easily understood explanations for its light-eating microbe story. That was always going to go down well with Tyson.
